INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus curiae Stephen Richer was the elected
Maricopa County Recorder from 2021 to 2025. In this
role, he was responsible for voter registration, early
voting administration, and public records in Maricopa
County, Arizona. He is currently a legal fellow with
the Cato Institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for
Constitutional Studies and a senior fellow at Harvard
Kennedy School’s Ash Center  for Democratic
Governance and Innovation. Amicus has an interest
in the p roper application of federal law to state and
local election administration.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The first Question Presented asks whether
Arizona may require documentary proof of citizenship
(“DPOC”) from applicants using its state -developed
mail voter registration form, or whether such a
requirement is prohibited by either a federal consent
decree or the National Voter Registration Act
(“NVRA”). This case is an unsuitable vehicle for
resolving the important NVRA issue left open by this
Court in Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona,

1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, counsel for amicus
certify that no party’s counsel authored this brief in whole or in
part; no party or party’s counsel contributed money that was
intended to fund the preparation or submission of the brief; and
no person other than amicus , their members, or their  counsel
contributed money intended to fund the preparation or
submission of the brief.

2

Inc. (“ITCA”), 570 U.S. 1 (2013): whether, and under
what circumstances,  the NVRA permits States to
require DPOC from applicants using state -developed
mail registration forms to register for federal
elections.
Resolution of that question may depend on the
application of the NVRA’s necessity requirement to
the particular circumstances of a State’s voter
registration system. Yet the unusual procedural
history of this case prevented the lower courts from
fully examining that potentially fact -bound inquiry.
Deciding the question on this record therefore risks
establishing a nationwide rule governing state voter
registration requirements without the factual and
legal development necessary to resolve an issue of
such consequence. Amicus  takes no position on the
consent-decree portion of the first Q uestion
Presented, nor the second Question Presented.
Accordingly, amicus urges the Court to dismiss
petitioner’s writ as improvidently granted insofar as
it concerns the NVRA portion of the first Question
Presented, allowing this important issue to develop
further in the lower courts. Alternatively, if the Court
wishes to reach the NVRA preemption question, it
should vacate and remand for  further factual and
legal development.

3

ARGUMENT
I. This case is an unsuitable vehicle for
resolving the important question of when
Arizona, and by i mplication every state,
may require documentary proof of
citizenship on state -developed mail voter
registration forms under the NVRA.
A. The question of whether, and under
what circumstances, the NVRA
permits documentary proof of
citizenship on S tate Forms remains
important and w arrants
consideration in a c ase that
squarely presents it.
Although this Court has addressed
documentary proof of citizenship requirements
imposed on applicants using the National Mail Voter
Registration Form (“Federal Form”), it has not
resolved the corresponding question for applicants
using a State’s own mail voter registration form
(“State Form”) to  register for federal elections.  In
ITCA, this Court held that, notwithstanding the state
DPOC law, Arizona must still permit voters who
submit the F ederal Form without DPOC to vote in
federal elections. ITCA, 570 U.S. at 12–13, 20. At the
same time, the Court recognized that States possess
authority to determine voter qualifications for federal
elections. Id. at 17. The Court also recognized that the

4

NVRA permits states to develop their own voter
registration forms  to register voters in state and
federal elections, which need not be identical to the
Federal Form, though the Federal Form “provides a
backstop.” Id. at 12.
ITCA did not decide , however, when a State
may require additional documentary proof of
citizenship as a condition of registering to vote in
federal elections through its own state mail
registration forms. Section 6 of the National Voter
Registration Act permits a State to “develop and use
a mail voter registration form ” to register voters for
federal elections, so long as the State Form “meets all
of the criteria stated in section 20508(b).” 52 U.S.C. §
20505(a)(2). Those criteria include Section 9’s
direction that a form “may require only  such
identifying information” and “other information” as is
“necessary to enable the appropriate State election
official to assess the eligibility of the applicant and to
administer voter registration .” Id. § 20508(b)(1)
(emphasis added) (“the NVRA necessity inquiry”) .2 It
separately requires an attestation that the applicant
meets each eligibility requirement, including
citizenship, signed under penalty of perjury. Id.  §
20508(b)(2). The question left open by ITCA , then, is
when DPOC, in addition to that sworn attestation, is

2 This brief refers to the NVRA’s necessity inquiry using various
formulations, including the “Section 9 necessity inquiry” and
the necessity inquiry under 52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)(1), all of which
refer to the same statutory inquiry.

5

“necessary” within the meaning of § 20508(b)(1) (“the
State Form DPOC question”).
B. Resolving the State Form DPOC
question may require courts to
determine whether the NVRA’s
necessity inquiry is a pure question
of law or is fact-bound.
Resolving whether the NVRA permits States to
require documentary proof of citizenship on state -
developed mail voter  registration forms may require
the Court to determine whether the necessity inquiry
is a pure question of law or depends at least in part on
factual questions concerning the State’s need for
documentary proof.
The proper interpretation of the NVRA’s
necessity requirement remains contested.  Having
already concluded that the LULAC Consent Decree
barred Arizona election officials from enforcing H.B.
2492’s DPOC requirement for State Form applicants,
the Ninth Circuit addressed the NVRA question only
as an alternative ground for its decision. Mi Familia
Vota v. Fontes, 129 F.4th 691, 717–20 (9th Cir. 2025).
In a brief analysis, the court interpreted  “necessary”
under 52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)(1) to mean “essential” and
concluded that Arizona could not require DPOC from
State Form applicants registering to vote only in
federal elections because the citizenship checkbox
already provided proof of citizenship  through an

6

attestation. Id. at 719–20.  In contrast , Professor
Michael Morley argues that “necessary” may mean
“convenient” or “useful,” rather than strictly
“essential.” Br. of Amici Curiae Professor Michael T.
Morley & Florida State University Election Law
Center in Support of  Neither Party at 23– 24,
Republican Nat’l Comm. v. Mi Familia Vota , No. 25-
1017 (filed Sept. 4, 2026) [hereinafter Morley Amicus
Br.].
However, even assuming arguendo the Ninth
Circuit’s interpretation of “necessary” as “essential,”
the legal meaning of that term is distinct from the
fact-bound question of whether DPOC is “essential”
under the circumstances of a particular State’s
registration system.  Determining whether DPOC is
necessary to enable state election officials to assess
eligibility and administer mail voter registration may
depend on evidence concerning the State’s actual need
for additional documentary proof. Such evidence could
include the State’s existing citizenship -verification
capabilities, the availability and reliability of
alternative sources of citizenship information, and the
practical consequences of relying on an attestation
alone. The State may also need to prove that there is
a particular factual reason in the state to be concerned
about noncitizen voting. Whether DPOC is necessary
under the particular circumstances of Arizona’s mail
registration system may therefore depend on
inferences drawn from competing evidence. See Ross
v. Day, 232 U.S. 110, 116 (1914) (noting the meaning

7

of a term in a statute is “a question of law,” but “the
drawing of correct inferences from the evidence”
regarding the statutory term is “a question of fact”).
The Tenth Circuit’s interpretation of  an
analogous NVRA provision illustrates why the
necessity inquiry may involve both legal and factual
questions. In Fish v. Kobach  (Fish I) , the court
considered whether Kansas could require DPOC from
applicants registering through the NVRA’s motor
voter process. 840 F.3d 710, 715 –16 (10th Cir. 2016).
The court held that a citizenship attestation under
penalty of perjury is presumptively sufficient under
the NVRA’s motor voter provisions, but that a State
may rebut that presumption through an adequate
factual showing. Id.  at 737– 39. To “rebut the
presumptive sufficiency ,” id. at 738, the court
required the State to demonstrate that “a substantial
number of noncitizens have successfully registered to
vote under the attestation requirement ,” id. at 739.
The Tenth Circuit thus recognized that whether an
attestation adequately enables election officials to
assess citizenship eligibility may depend on evidence
of an actual problem with noncitizen registration in
the State, rather than speculation about the
possibility of such registration.
In Fish v. Schwab, the Tenth Circuit reaffirmed
the distinction between interpreting the statutory
requirement and determining whether it is satisfied
in practice made by Fish I. 957 F.3d 1105, 1141– 44

8

(10th Cir. 2020). As that court explained, “whether the
attestation requirement actually satisfies the
minimum-information principle in a given case turns
on the factual question of whether the attestation
requirement is sufficient for a state to carry out these
duties.” Id. at 1114 (quoting Fish I, 840 F.3d at 738)
(emphasis added).
Although the Fish decisions concerned Section
5 of the NVRA’s motor voter requirements,  52 U.S.C.
§ 20504(c)(2)(B),  rather than the State Form
provisions governed by Sections 6 and 9,  id. §§
20505(a)(2), 20508(b)(1),  the decisions illustrate the
distinction between interpreting a statutory necessity
requirement and determining whether that
requirement is satisfied under a particular State’s
circumstances. Whether Section 9 requires precisely
the evidentiary showing articulated in Fish I remains
an open question. But the Fish decisions demonstrate
why a court considering whether DPOC is necessary
may need to examine evidence of noncitizen
registration notwithstanding existing attestations,
alongside the effectiveness of alternative verification
procedures, before determining whether add itional
documentation is justified.
Ultimately, this Court should not use this case
to resolve the competing interpretations of
“necessary,” nor determine whether the NVRA’s
necessity inquiry is purely legal or depends in part on
factual questions. Whether, and under what

9

circumstances, the NVRA permits States to require
DPOC on State Forms is an important question that
warrants eventual resolution. But the importance of
that question counsels in favor of addressing it in a
case that squarely presents the issue and permits
consideration of the factual circumstances that may
bear on its application.  See The Monrosa v. Carbon
Black Export, Inc., 359 U.S. 180, 184 (1959) (stating
that resolution of an important legal question could
“await a day when the issue is posed less abstractly.”).
As explained in the next section, the unusual
procedural history of this litigation and the absence of
findings directed toward the State Form necessity
inquiry make this case an unsuitable vehicle for
establishing a nationwide rule.
C. The unusual procedural history of
this case prevented the lower courts
from directly resolving the
potentially fact- bound question of
whether DPOC is necessary in
Arizona’s actual registration
system.
The State Form DPOC dispute arises against
the backdrop of a preexisting consent decree that
independently governs Arizona ’s voter registration
procedures.  Arizona has long required voters to
provide DPOC to register to vote  in state and local
elections. See ITCA , 570 U.S. at 6.  Following this
Court’s decision in ITCA , Arizona maintained a two -

10

track registration system under which applicants
submitting the Federal Form without DPOC could
register to vote in  federal elections, while applicants
submitting the State Form without DP OC were
rejected. See Mi Familia Vota, 129 F.4th at 703.
In 2017, the League of United Latin American
Citizens Arizona (“LULAC”) and Arizona Students’
Association (“ASA”) challenged this two- track regime
as unconstitutional. See Compl. ¶¶ 78–88, League of
United Latin Am.  Citizens Ariz. v. Reagan, No. 2:17-
cv-04102 (D. Ariz.  Nov. 7, 2017) , ECF No. 1 . The
parties agreed to the entry of a consent decree  (the
“LULAC Consent Decree”) , Pet. App. 474a , which
required, among other things, that the Secretary
“provide guidance to the County Recorders to accept
State Form applications submitted without DPOC,”
Pet. App. 484a. The Secretary of State of Arizona (the
“Secretary”) also agreed “to treat State Form
applications exactly as they treat Federal Form
applications.” Pet. App. 476a . In 2022, the Arizona
legislature passed House Bill 2492, which, as relevant
here, required registrars to reject S tate Form
applications that lacked DPOC, even if the applicant
would be federally eligible using the Federal Form. Ariz.
Rev. Stat. Ann. § 16-121.01(A), (C); see also Mi Familia
Vota, 129 F.4th at 704–05. H.B. 2492 thus directs the
Secretary to violate the LULAC Consent Decree.
Multiple plaintiff groups filed suit. Specifically, the
LULAC, ASA, and Living United for Change in
Arizona (collectively, the LUCHA Plaintiffs)

11

challenged the law in Living United for Change in
Ariz. v. Hobbs, No. 2:22 -cv-00519 (D. Ariz. Mar. 31,
2022). That action was consolidated with Mi Familia
Vota v. Fontes, No. 2:22 -cv-00509 (D. Ariz. May 1 7,
2022), ECF No. 39 . The se cases named the Arizona
Secretary of State and Attorney General as defendants.
The Republican National Committee (“RNC”)
subsequently intervened in another challenge that
was consolidated into the same proceedings . See
Democratic Nat’l Comm. v. Hobbs, No. 2:22 -cv-01369
(D. Ariz. Aug. 24, 2022), ECF No. 18; Mi Familia Vota
v. Fontes, No. 2:22-cv-00509 (D. Ariz. Aug. 24 , 2022),
ECF No. 91.
The consolidated cases proceeded to motions for
partial summary judgment as part of the initial
proceedings. The RNC moved for partial summary
judgment on the NVRA claims; however, the LUCHA
Plaintiffs opposed, including on the ground that the
NVRA claims related to DPOC required further
factual development. See LUCHA Pls.’ Resp. to Defs.’
Mot. for Summ. J. & Cross-Mot. for Partial Summ. J.
at 1 n.2, 2, 13–14, Mi Familia Vota v. Fontes, No. 2:22-
cv-00509 (D. Ariz. June 5, 2023), ECF No. 394.  The
district court nevertheless granted summary judgment
for plaintiffs on the NVRA claims related to State
Form DPOC on a ground no party had briefed: that
the claim “is resolved by the existing LULAC Consent
Decree” because the decree “reflects that Arizona
agreed to refrain from precisely the conduct that the
RNC would have Arizona participate in.” Mi Familia

12

Vota v. Fontes, 691 F.  Supp. 3d 1077, 1096 (D. Ariz.
2023). The court held that the decree “precludes Arizona
from enforcing H.B. 2492’s mandate to reject any
State Form without accompanying DPOC,” entered
declaratory judgment to that effect, and issued a
permanent injunction. Id.  at 1103– 04. Only in a
footnote did the court reach the theory that the parties
had actually briefed, holding in the alternative that
H.B. 2492 ’s State Form DPOC requirement also
violated Section 6 of the NVRA . Id. at 1096 n.13.
Although the district court later more fully considered
the NVRA necessity inquiry following a bench trial, it
addressed that inquiry’s  application only to the
requirement that State Form users submit proof-ofresidency, not State Form DPOC requirements. See
Mi Familia Vota v. Fontes, 719 F.  Supp. 3d 929, 950
n.10, 996 (D. Ariz. 2024).
The district court thus resolved the State Form
DPOC challenge without separately determining, on
a record developed for that purpose, whether DPOC
was necessary, under Section 9 of the NVRA, to assess
eligibility under Arizona’s actual registration
procedures. Its disposition rested principally on the
consent decree, which  provided an independent
ground for prohibiting rejection of otherwise eligible
State Form applicants without DPOC. Although the
court briefly addressed the NVRA in the alternative,
it did not make findings specifically directed toward
whether Arizona’s existing citizenship attestations,
verification systems, and alternative sources of

13

citizenship information were sufficient to assess
eligibility without additional documentary proof. Nor
did it make findings directed toward whether noncitizen
registration notwithstanding those safeguards
established a particularized need for DPOC. The
potentially fact -bound application of Section 9’s
necessity requirement therefore remained unresolved
in the district court.
The Ninth Circuit likewise treated  the NVRA
necessity inquiry as a purely legal question, without
separately examining whether DPOC was necessary
under the circumstances of Arizona’s voter
registration system. The court affirmed the district
court’s conclusion that the  LULAC Consent Decree
barred Arizona election officials from enforcing H.B.
2492’s requirement that State Form applicants
provide DPOC. Mi Familia Vota, 129 F.4th at 717–19.
It then held, in the alternative, that the NVRA ,
through the Section 9 necessity inquiry, as
incorporated by reference in Section 6, independently
prohibited Arizona from requiring DPOC from State
Form applicants registering to vote only in federal
elections. Id. at 719–20. As discussed above, the court
treated the issue as a purely legal question,
concluding that “[o]ur inquiry ends here because the
text of the NVRA is unambiguous.” Id. It therefore did
not separately consider whether evidence concerning
Arizona’s existing registration procedures, the
effectiveness of citizenship attestations, or the State’s
ability to verify citizenship through other means
might bear on whether DPOC was necessary.

14

Consequently, neither lower court resolved,
through findings directed toward the NVRA necessity
inquiry as applied to State Form DPOC requirements,
whether additional documentary proof was necessary
under the circumstances presented. Whatever the
correct ultimate interpretation of the NVRA, the
absence of lower -court consideration of these factual
questions makes this case an unsuitable vehicle for
establishing a nationwide rule governing DPOC
requirements on state -developed mail voter
registration forms.
D. Better vehicles for deciding the
State Form DPOC question are
likely to arise and may already be
percolating in the lower courts.
The statutory question underlying the
necessity inquiry in Section 9 of the NVRA warrants
resolution in a case that permits the Court to consider
both the governing legal standard and, if relevant, the
factual circumstances necessary to apply it.   Ideally,
such a case would involve a direct legal analysis of the
NVRA’s necessity inquiry and direct application of
that inquiry to State Form DPOC requirements in the
lower courts. This type of vehicle would allow the
Court to draw on the lower courts’ full merits
decisions in resolving the statutory questions at hand
and, if the NVRA’s necessity inquiry is indeed fact -
bound, to rely on a fully developed factual record in
applying the governing standard.

15

Cases of this kind  are already percolating in
the lower courts. In April 2026, Florida enacted H.B.
991, which will require documentary proof of
citizenship from certain registrants and voters whose
citizenship cannot be verified through state records .
See Act of Apr. 1, 2026,  Ch. 2026-26, § 4, 2026 Fla.
Laws ___ (amending Fla. Stat. § 97.053 (2025)).
Several p laintiffs have since challenged this law
under Section 9 of the NVRA, alleging that H.B. 991
violates § 20508(b) because “additional proof of
citizenship is not ‘necessary’ to assess prospective
voters’ eligibility.” Am. Compl. ¶ 161, Fla. State Conf.
of Branches & Youth Units of the NAACP v. Byrd, No.
1:26-cv-22257-JB (S.D. Fla. filed July 22, 2026) , ECF
No. 90 (quoting 52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)); see also Compl.
¶ 123, Black Voters Matter Fund v. Byrd, No. 1:26-cv-
26047 (S.D. Fla. filed Sept. 1, 2026).  Unlike the
instant case, these cases do not arise against the
backdrop of a preexisting consent decree and therefore
may permit direct consideration of the “necessity”
inquiry required under § 20508(b)(1)  and the
statutory limits on additional documentation required
for State Form registration.
Although the Florida litigation remains at an
early stage and may not ultimately prove to be a
suitable vehicle for review, it illustrates a  key point:
The instant case is not the only avenue for addressing
the scope and meaning of the NVRA as applied to
State Form DPOC requirements. Given the
significance of this issue, litigation that presents the

16

NVRA question more directly and in a more suitable
procedural posture is likely to arise.
II. The Court should dismiss the writ as
improvidently granted rather than
establish a nationwide rule concerning
State Form DPOC requirements on this
record.
A. The Court has dismissed writs as
improvidently granted when
important questions arise in cases
that cannot adequately resolve
them.
The Cour t has long exercised its authority to
dismiss a writ as improvidently granted when a
“mare’s nest could stand in the way of [it] reaching the
question presented on which [it] granted certiorari, or
at the very least, complicate [its] resolution of that
question.” See Arizona v. City and C ounty of San
Francisco, 596 U.S. 763, 766 (2022 ) (Roberts, C.J.,
concurring); accord The Monrosa,  359 U.S. at 183
(noting that the Court dismisses cases as
improvidently granted when there are
“circumstances” that were “not . . . fully apprehended
at the time certiorari was granted”).
Among the recurring “mare’s nest[s],” Arizona,
596 U.S. at 766, that prompt the Court to dismiss a
writ as improvidently granted is the discovery that
“[a]n important issue [is] found not to be presented by

17

the record.” Stephen M. Shapiro et al., Supreme Court
Practice ch. 5, § 15 (11th ed. 2019).  In Johnson v.
Massachusetts, for example, the Court dismissed a
writ as improvidently granted because the “record
relevant to the constitutional claims . . . asserted [was]
insufficient to permit decision of those claims.” 390
U.S. 511, 511 (1968). The Court did likewise in Belcher
v. Stengel , noting that “the question framed in the
petition for certiorari [was] not in fact presented by
the record.” 429 U.S. 118, 119 (1976).
Dismissal of a case as improvidently granted
does not constitute a decision on the merits or imply
approval or disapproval of the lower court’s reasoning.
See Hodges v. United States, 368 U.S. 139, 140 (1961).
Rather, the lower court decision in the matter simply
remains in place.
B. The instant matter bears the
hallmarks of a case in which the
writ of certiorari  should be
dismissed as improvidently granted.
A “mare’s nest ,” Arizona, 596 U.S. at 766,
stands in the way of the Court reaching  the question
of whether the NVRA p reempts State Form DPOC
requirements via the instant case . As explained in
Part I, the unusual procedural posture of this case has
left the lower -court opinions without findings
specifically directed to the NVRA’s  necessity inquiry,
see 52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)(1),  as applied to State Form

18

DPOC requirements. See supra Part I.C. The district
court’s analysis rested almost entirely on the LULAC
consent decree and the Ninth Circuit treated the
necessity inquiry , which it only reached in the
alternative to the Consent Decree question,  as a
question of pure law rather than one of mixed fact and
law. Id.
The parties’ briefing reflects the same gap :
nearly all the  briefs filed by petitioner and
respondents treat the NVRA’s necessity inquiry as a
question of law requiring  the Court to formulate  a
categorical legal rule, giving no consideration to
whether § 20508(b)(1) calls for a fact -bound inquiry.
See Br. for Pet’r at 18–27, Republican Nat’l Comm. v.

(failing to address the meaning of “necessary”
altogether). But see Br. for Resp’ts State of Ariz. & Its
Att’y Gen . in Partial Support of Pet ’r at 15– 17, Mi
Familia Vota , No. 25 -1017 (filed Aug. 28, 2026)

19

(granting implicitly that the NVRA’s necessity inquiry
may be fact -bound because it incorporates Arizona
state law).
The resulting gaps are consequential. Insofar
as the Court must authoritatively interpret the NVRA
necessity inquiry , it  has little reasoning from lower
courts and little briefing to draw on to decide whether
that inquiry is purely legal or fact -bound. And if the
inquiry is fact-bound, the record likewise provides no
adequate basis for  determining the evidentiary
showing a State must make to establish that
documentary proof is necessary to assess voter
eligibility. As in Johnson v. Massachusetts, the “record
relevant to the” question at hand may therefore be
“insufficient to permit decision of [that question].” 390
U.S. at 511.
In light of the insufficiency of the record ,
amicus urges the Court to dismiss as improvidently
granted insofar as it concerns the question of whether
the NVRA p reempts State Form DPOC
requirements.3 Although this course of action would
leave the Ninth Circuit’s interpretation of the NVRA’s
necessity inquiry intact, its effect would go no further:
The interpretation would remain binding only within
the Ninth Circuit. The Court would not have to
establish a nationwide rule concerning the NVRA and

20

State Form DPOC requirements without the benefit
of lower-court analysis, a developed evidentiary
record, or full adversarial briefing on important
aspects of that question.
C. The national importance of the State
Form DPOC  question further
justifies permitting additional lower
court consideration of this issue.
The case for dismissing  the NVRA portion of
the first question presented in  the instant case  as
improvidently granted is particularly strong given the
national significance of the question presented : The
Court’s decision could  affect voter registration
practices in every State. Given these stakes, it would
be prudent for  the Court to allow lower courts to
percolate on the necessity inquiry in  § 20508(b)(1)
before laying down a rule itself. The lower courts could
explore, for example,  whether the necessity inquiry
calls for a categorical legal rule, an evidentiary
showing, or factual development that accounts for
differences among States’ registration systems and
relevant facts about evidence of problems with
noncitizen voting. See supra Part I.B. The Court could
then draw on the  reasoning in these decisions when
ultimately resolving this nationally significant
question in a more appropriate vehicle.
At bottom, the question presented need not be
resolved now as a binary choice between permitting

21

every State to require DPOC and categorically
prohibiting such requirements.  Further litigation
could clarify whether the NVRA’s necessity inquiry
instead calls for a more nuanced standard. Dismissing
part of petitioner’s writ as improvidently granted
would allow the lower courts to develop the
jurisprudence without foreclosing the possibility that
DPOC may be necessary in particular circumstances,
or that States may indeed possess unrestricted
authority to impose such requirements. The Court
would thus preserve its ability to resolve the question
with the benefit of further judicial consideration.
III. Alternatively, if the Court determines that
applying the NVRA ’s necessity inq uiry
calls for additional factfinding, it should
vacate and remand for further
proceedings.
While amicus urges the Court to dismiss part
of petitioner’s writ as improvidently granted, if the
Court instead concludes that the NVRA’s  necessity
inquiry is fact-bound, it should vacate and remand for
further proceedings, rather than reach a conclusion on
the existing record.
The Court has long emphasized  that it is a
“court of review, not of first view.” Cutter v. Wilkinson,
544 U.S. 709, 718 n.7 (2005).  Accordingly, the Court
avoids applying law to facts in the first instance ,
especially when the factual record is underdeveloped.

22

See, e.g. , Int’l Primate Prot. League v. Adm’ rs of
Tulane Educ. Fund, 500 U.S. 72, 89 (1991) (“This
mixed question of law and fact should not be resolved
in the first instance by this Court, least of all without
an appropriate record.”); CRST Van Expedited, Inc. v.
E.E.O.C., 578 U.S. 419, 435 (2016) (“It is not the
Court’s usual practice to adjudicate either legal or
predicate factual questions in the first instance.”).
If the Court determines that the NVRA
necessity inquiry is fact-bound, deciding whether the
NVRA preempts Arizona’s State Form DPOC
requirement would require the Court to resolve a
mixed question of law and fact in the first instance .
Although the district court, following a bench trial,
made factual findings con cerning Arizona’s voter
registration procedures and the rarity of noncitizen
voting in the state, see Mi Familia Vota, 719 F. Supp.
3d at 953– 67 (noting that “non- citizens voting in
Arizona is quite rare, and non- citizen voter fraud in
Arizona is rarer still,” id. at 967), it did not apply those
findings to determine whether the NVRA requires or
permits Arizona’s State Form DPOC requirements
under the circumstances of its registration system.
See supra Part I.C. Instead, the court’s disposition of
the DPOC challenge rested principally on the LULAC
Consent Decree, while its separate analysis of the
necessity requirement concerned proof of residency.
See Mi Familia Vota, 719 F. Supp. 3d at 996. Nor did
the district court consider whether additional fact -
finding was needed to conduct the necessity inquiry

23

that Section 9 of the NVRA  potentially requires. The
Ninth Circuit  likewise treated  the NVRA necessity
inquiry as a pure question of statutory interpretation,
with no fact-bound component. See Mi Familia Vota, 129
F.4th at 719–20. Neither court, therefore, specifically
determined whether, in light of  existing citizenship
attestations and verification procedures , Arizona’s
State Form DPOC requirement was “necessary”
under the circumstances of the State’s registration
system and databases. If the Court has to decide that
question, it would be doing so in the first instance.
Consequently, if the Court finds that Section 9
of the NVRA requires resolution of a mixed question
of law and fact, it should vacate the  Ninth Circuit’s
judgment and remand for  the district court to
determine, in the first instance, whether DPOC is
necessary to enable Arizona election officials to
assess voter eligibility and administer registration.
On remand, t he parties could develop evidence
concerning the effectiveness of citizenship
attestations, existing methods of independently
verifying citizenship, the structure of the State’ s
DPOC requirement, and whether additional
documentation is needed to assess voter eligibility .
They could also adduce evidence of any existing
problems with noncitizen registration. Compare
Morley Amicus Br . at 4– 11 (collecting reporting on
voter registration by alleged noncitizens in half a
dozen states, not including Arizona), with

(reporting that only eight of 60 suspected noncitizen

and the fact -bound question of whether DPOC is
necessary in the context of Arizona’s actual

In sum, if the Court concludes that application
of the necessity provision requires factual findings not
made below, it should vacate and remand for further
proceedings. Amicus nevertheless maintains that
dismissal as improvidently granted is  the preferable
disposition because it would preserve the opportunity
to resolve the important statutory question in a case
that squarely presents it on a more suitable record.
